You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write an essay of up to 500 words on why most product roadmaps fail.

=== TEXT A ===
## Why Most Product Roadmaps Fail

Product roadmaps often fail because they are asked to do something impossible: make an uncertain future look certain. A tidy sequence of features and release dates creates confidence, but it can hide the assumptions, trade-offs, and unanswered questions that determine whether a product succeeds.

The first problem is confusing delivery with progress. A roadmap might promise a redesigned dashboard, a mobile app, and three integrations. Shipping all five does not necessarily make the product more useful or the business more sustainable. When teams are judged by whether they deliver planned features, they optimize for completion rather than impact. The roadmap becomes a checklist instead of a strategy.

The second problem is premature commitment. Early estimates are made when teams know the least about technical complexity, customer needs, and dependencies. Yet tentative dates can quickly become sales promises, budget assumptions, and executive expectations. As evidence accumulates, changing direction becomes politically expensive. Teams continue building something questionable because removing it would look like failure—even when stopping would be the better decision.

Roadmaps also fail when they substitute negotiation for prioritization. Sales wants features that close deals. Support wants recurring complaints resolved. Leadership wants visible growth initiatives. Engineering wants to reduce technical debt. Each request may be reasonable, but combining them does not automatically produce a coherent plan. Without a clear target customer, desired outcome, and basis for saying no, the roadmap becomes a record of who argued most effectively.

Another weakness is treating the roadmap as a document rather than an ongoing decision process. Customer behavior changes, competitors move, and experiments disprove assumptions. A plan that cannot absorb those discoveries becomes obsolete. But constant, unexplained changes are equally damaging: they leave teams distracted and stakeholders distrustful. Adaptability requires both regular review and a clear explanation of what changed and why.

Better roadmaps do not eliminate uncertainty; they make it manageable. They connect proposed work to measurable outcomes, distinguish near-term commitments from longer-term possibilities, and identify assumptions that need testing. They also acknowledge capacity constraints and leave room for maintenance, discovery, and unexpected problems.

Most importantly, a useful roadmap communicates choices rather than merely announcing activity. It explains which problems matter now, why they matter, and what evidence would justify a different direction.

A roadmap fails when following it becomes more important than achieving its purpose. It succeeds when it helps an organization coordinate its efforts while preserving the ability to learn. The goal is not to predict every turn in the road, but to keep moving toward a destination worth reaching.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
Most product roadmaps fail because they make uncertain work look certain. A row of features arranged neatly across four quarters suggests that a team knows what customers will need, how long development will take, and what the business should prioritize months from now. Usually, it knows much less than the roadmap implies.

The trouble often starts with the question the roadmap is meant to answer. Instead of asking which customer problems matter most, teams ask what they can promise to deliver. Sales wants a feature that might close a deal. Leadership wants something impressive for the next board meeting. Existing customers want their requests acknowledged. The roadmap becomes a negotiated settlement between stakeholders rather than a coherent plan for improving the product.

Once those promises acquire dates, changing direction gets harder. A team may discover that customers do not care about a planned feature, or that a simpler solution would work better. But removing the feature now looks like breaking a commitment. People keep building because the roadmap says they should, even when the original reason for building has disappeared. The plan survives at the expense of its purpose.

Roadmaps also tend to confuse shipping with success. Launching a dashboard is easy to recognize as a completed task. Helping customers make better decisions is harder to measure and may require several attempts. When delivery is the main measure of progress, teams have an incentive to finish what they listed, not to investigate whether it helped. A roadmap can be completed on schedule while the product barely improves.

Then there is the work that never makes it onto the slide: maintenance, security fixes, support, hiring, technical dependencies, and the unexpected complexity of changing an established system. Plans built around uninterrupted development are already behind before anyone starts. Adding more detail rarely fixes this. It can simply make unrealistic assumptions look more convincing.

A useful roadmap does not eliminate uncertainty. It makes uncertainty visible. It explains which problems deserve attention, why they matter, and what evidence would justify changing course. Near-term commitments can be specific, while later work remains provisional. It leaves room for the less glamorous work that keeps a product reliable.

The real test of a roadmap is not whether the team follows it exactly. It is whether it helps people make better decisions as they learn. Most roadmaps fail when they stop being tools for those decisions and become promises nobody feels allowed to question.
=== END OF TEXT B ===

Frequent negative parallelism ('checklist instead of a strategy', 'document rather than an ongoing decision process', 'choices rather than merely announcing activity', 'not to predict... but to keep moving') (Tell 1)
